passage: My name is Harsha, and for three months Gargi has messaged me at all hours. Last night her voice note arrived at 1 a.m., and I listened with my eyes half shut because I had a chemistry test at eight. I love her. She told me something heavy about her home and said I was the only one she could trust. But lately I answer with just "hmm" and "ok", and then feel guilty and resentful in the same breath. Today I finally said, "I want to be there for you, but I can't be your only person, and I can't reply after ten." She looked hurt. I suggested her aunt, and the school counsellor too. She said she would think about it.

qa.q: What time did Gargi's voice note arrive last night?
qa.a: Her voice note arrived at 1 a.m.

qa.q: What was Harsha feeling about the late-night messages, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Harsha was worn out and a little resentful while still caring; the "hmm" and "ok" replies and the guilt in the same breath show it.

qa.q: What would you advise Harsha to do if Gargi keeps messaging late at night?
qa.a: Keep the limit kindly, and gently repeat the idea of talking to her aunt or the school counsellor.

qa.q: How might Gargi have felt when Harsha set the limit?
qa.a: Gargi looked hurt, and may have feared losing the one person she trusts, though saying she would think about it shows the idea did not fall on deaf ears.

grounding: Harsha is worn out by a friend's constant heavy confiding, sets a limit and points to a counsellor and family.

passage:
Dear Madhuri,
Sorry this is a letter, but I can't say it in the corridor. Today Kabir and a few others kept guessing who writes the poems in the class notebook. They teased me, "Come on, Vandana, you know!" One even hid my geometry box until I answered. I said nothing, and it felt good and awful at once. Your secret is yours to tell. But I want to ask: does hiding it bother you? You look happy when you write, yet you flinch when anyone reads a poem aloud. If you ever want to share them, I'll sit beside you. If not, my lips stay shut. 🙂
Your friend,
Vandana

qa.q: What did one classmate hide until Vandana answered?
qa.a: One classmate hid Vandana's geometry box until Vandana answered.

qa.q: What does Vandana think about the secret, and what worry sits beside that loyalty?
qa.a: Vandana thinks the secret is Madhuri's to tell, but wonders whether hiding it bothers Madhuri, since Madhuri flinches when a poem is read aloud.

qa.q: What could Vandana do next to check the secret is not hurting Madhuri?
qa.a: Ask Madhuri privately how it feels, and offer to sit beside Madhuri if Madhuri ever wants to share the poems. 😊

qa.q: How might Madhuri feel on reading this letter?
qa.a: Probably relieved that Vandana stayed loyal, and maybe a little exposed at being asked; the flinch at hearing a poem aloud shows the secret still matters.

grounding: Vandana keeps a friend's harmless secret through teasing and checks in that it is not weighing on the friend.

passage: Every afternoon in the colony park, Damini waited on the bench under the banyan tree with a story ready. "You're my hero, Tanvir," Damini said again, and told of a fight with a cousin, a small lie to a teacher, a fear of the maths exam. Tanvir felt taller and heavier at the same time. Then Damini said, "I'll do whatever you say," and Tanvir caught a small, pleased thought about simply deciding things for Damini. Tanvir swallowed it. "I lose my keys, I copy homework sometimes. I'm not a hero," Tanvir said. "Tell your didi about the maths fear too. And your teacher. I'll listen, but I'm not the only person." Damini frowned, then nodded slowly.

qa.q: Where did Damini wait for Tanvir every afternoon?
qa.a: Damini waited on the bench under the banyan tree in the colony park.

qa.q: What did Tanvir feel when Damini said "I'll do whatever you say"?
qa.a: Tanvir felt pleased and tempted to decide things for Damini, then uneasy enough to swallow that thought; feeling "taller and heavier at the same time" shows the mix of pride and pressure.

qa.q: What could Tanvir keep doing so Damini has other support too?
qa.a: Keep being honest about flaws and keep pointing Damini to the didi and the teacher, while still listening.

qa.q: How might Damini see Tanvir's answer?
qa.a: Damini frowned first, so may have been a little disappointed, but the slow nod suggests Damini can see Tanvir is being honest and caring.

grounding: A younger friend idolises Tanvir and shares everything; Tanvir feels proud and pressured and stays honest, pointing to other support.

passage: The music at the school fair was so loud that Zainab had to lean in to hear anything. With three minutes left before their ring-toss stall opened, Aditi held up a phone and grinned. "One selfie for the class group. Squeeze in!" Zainab's ears went hot. "No photo, thanks," Zainab said. Aditi's smile dropped. Zainab's mouth opened to add "sorry, my hair is a mess, sorry", but Zainab stopped and said only, "It's just a no. Not about you." The pause lasted as long as one line of the song. Then Aditi lowered the phone. "Okay. Fair." A second later: "Can you hold the rings while I count the prizes?" Zainab nodded, shoulders loosening.

qa.q: How many minutes were left before the ring-toss stall opened?
qa.a: Three minutes were left before their ring-toss stall opened.

qa.q: What was Zainab feeling right after Aditi's smile dropped?
qa.a: Zainab felt awkward and tempted to apologise; the hot ears and the nearly-said "sorry, my hair is a mess" show it.

qa.q: What would you advise Zainab if a friend keeps asking for the photo?
qa.a: Repeat calmly that it is a no, without needing a reason, and stay friendly about everything else.

qa.q: How might Aditi have felt during that pause?
qa.a: Probably a bit hurt or embarrassed, since the smile dropped, but "Okay. Fair." and the new task show Aditi accepted it and moved on.

grounding: Zainab says no to a photo without apologising and the friend accepts it despite the awkward moment.

passage: After practice at the sports club, Yash, a senior from the under-19 squad, sat down beside Rashmi on the bench. "You're not like the other juniors. So mature. Come to the back of the pavilion, just us, and don't tell anyone." The flattery felt warm, and that was what confused Rashmi. Then: "If you really liked me, you wouldn't need to think about it." Rashmi's stomach tightened. "No," Rashmi said, standing. "That's enough of an answer." With shaky legs, Rashmi walked straight to the coach's office and told everything, including the part about not telling anyone. The coach listened, thanked Rashmi for coming, and said it was not Rashmi's fault. Then, with Rashmi still in the office, the coach phoned the club's safeguarding lead and Rashmi's parents.

qa.q: Where did Yash ask Rashmi to go, and what else did Yash ask?
qa.a: Yash asked Rashmi to come to the back of the pavilion, just us, and not to tell anyone.

qa.q: What was Rashmi feeling as Yash kept talking, and what shows it?
qa.a: Rashmi felt warmed by the flattery yet uneasy; the tightened stomach and shaky legs show the unease.

qa.q: What would you advise Rashmi if Yash keeps approaching after this?
qa.a: Keep saying no, stay near other people, and keep telling the coach or another trusted adult. 🤍

qa.q: How might the coach see Rashmi's decision to come forward?
qa.a: As a sensible and brave step; the coach thanked Rashmi and said it was not Rashmi's fault.

grounding: An older teen flatters and pressures Rashmi, who says no, leaves and tells a trusted adult who says it is not Rashmi's fault.

passage: Farhan, sit down. I'll tell you something from when I was fifteen, now that you've got your first phone. I'm Ganga, remember? A group at my school kept saying, "Send us a private picture, everyone does." They teased me too: "Still no boyfriend? What's wrong with you?" I laughed it off for weeks, then felt sick every time my phone buzzed. One evening a girl said she would show everyone my messages unless I sent something. My hands went cold, but I thought, these are mine. I sent nothing. That night I told my mother, and she went to the principal with me. The teasing died down after that.

qa.q: How old was Ganga when the group started asking for a private picture?
qa.a: Ganga was fifteen.

qa.q: What was Ganga feeling when a girl threatened to show everyone the messages?
qa.a: Ganga was frightened, with cold hands, yet clear that the pictures and messages were Ganga's own.

qa.q: What could Farhan do if a group pushes for private pictures?
qa.a: Send nothing, and tell a trusted adult, especially if anyone threatens to spread messages, as Ganga did with Ganga's mother.

qa.q: How might Ganga's mother have seen Ganga coming to her?
qa.a: Likely with worry but also trust; she went to the principal with Ganga straight away, which shows she took it seriously and stood beside Ganga.

grounding: Ganga recalls friends demanding private pictures and teasing, refusing to send anything and telling an adult when threatened.

passage: The mock paper lay folded in Hana's schoolbag for two nights, a red mark at the top low enough to hurt. Hana's father, Anders, had cut back on holidays to pay for the evening tutor, and every time he asked "How is it going?" Hana's throat closed. On the third evening Hana laid the paper on the kitchen table in Gothenburg. "Pappa, I have to show you something." Anders read it in silence. "I'm scared," Hana said. "You've spent so much on the tutor. I can try harder, but I can't carry all of it. If I fail, I need you still on my side." Anders took off his glasses. "I didn't know it felt that heavy," he said. "Let's make a plan, together."

qa.q: For how long was the mock paper hidden in Hana's schoolbag?
qa.a: The mock paper lay folded in Hana's schoolbag for two nights.

qa.q: What was Hana afraid of when thinking about the result?
qa.a: Hana was afraid of letting down Anders after he spent so much on the tutor, and of losing his support if Hana failed.

qa.q: What might have gone wrong if Hana had kept hiding the mock paper?
qa.a: The fear would probably have grown, and the secret could have exploded later at a worse moment, for both Hana and Anders.

qa.q: What was Anders thinking as he took off his glasses?
qa.a: Anders seemed surprised and sorry, realising his hopes felt "that heavy" to Hana, and wanted to help with a plan.

grounding: Hana dreads the result because the parent has spent savings, and tells the father plainly how much can be carried instead of hiding the mock score.

passage:
Zainab set the report card beside the dal. "Eighty-two? Last time it was ninety-one."
"It was a hard paper, Ammi."
"Board exams are in four months, Rehana."
Rehana stared at the rice. "I feel like you only smile when I score."
"That is not fair." Silence. Then, quieter: "I'm scared, beta. I never got to study past tenth. I don't want you to lose choices."
Rehana's shoulders dropped. "I hear that. But it helps when we make a weekly plan together. And when Friday nights are calm, with no marks talk."
"Friday nights, fine." Zainab slid the plate closer. "Plan tomorrow?"
"Okay, Ammi. Thank you."

qa.q: What marks did Rehana score, and what was the last score?
qa.a: Rehana scored eighty-two, and last time it was ninety-one.

qa.q: What does Rehana's staring at the rice suggest about how Rehana felt after the marks question?
qa.a: It suggests hurt and a pull to shut down, since Rehana then says "I feel like you only smile when I score."

qa.q: Which choice helped in this conversation, and why?
qa.a: Rehana listened to the fear behind the push and then asked for a weekly plan and calm Friday nights, so the talk turned from blame to a shared step.

qa.q: What is Ammi feeling underneath the push about marks?
qa.a: Fear that Rehana will lose choices; Ammi says "I'm scared" and mentions never getting to study past tenth. ❤️

grounding: Rehana feels measured by marks, hears the parent's fear behind the push and says what would help instead of shutting down.
